title: Seeds and records
bodyMd:
A neighbourhood seed exchange originally accepted packets labelled only with the plant name. Over time, volunteers noticed that gardeners struggled to interpret the results: a variety that thrived in one garden sometimes failed in another. They began inviting donors to record soil conditions, watering practices and the season in which the seeds had been collected. The extra information did not guarantee success, but it helped recipients choose more suitable varieties and interpret failures.

Some donors worried that detailed forms would discourage participation. The organisers therefore made the records optional and kept a short version for beginners. They described the exchange as a growing conversation rather than a catalogue of certified products. A packet carried both a biological possibility and a partial account of someone’s experience. The aim was not to eliminate uncertainty, but to make it easier for gardeners to learn from it.
